title: Prostration verses
hook: places marked in the mushaf where the reciter prostrates

segments.voice: Yesterday, hafiz: the ones who keep the whole Qur'an by heart. Your line was carried by heart. Did your new verse come back to you at an odd moment? Day three hundred twenty-four.

Imagine you're in a mosque, listening to the imam recite. Suddenly, in the middle of a surah, without a word of warning, he goes down: forehead to the floor. And the whole room goes with him. A few seconds later everyone rises, and the recitation carries on as if nothing happened. If you didn't know, you'd be left wondering what you'd missed. You missed a verse that bows. Today: prostration verses.
screen: `MID-SURAH, HE GOES DOWN.` → `THE WHOLE ROOM GOES WITH HIM.` → `A VERSE THAT BOWS.`

segments.voice: Scattered through the Qur'an are places where the text itself speaks of bowing down: the angels, the stars and the trees, the prophets, the believers who fall down in prostration when the verses are recited to them. At such places the Prophet ﷺ would prostrate when he recited or heard them. It's called the prostration of recitation, and the verses are called sajdah verses. Sajdah means a single prostration, from the same root as masjid, a mosque: the place of prostration. How many are there? Fourteen or fifteen, depending on the school of law. The schools also differ on whether it's required. Most scholars hold it's a strongly encouraged sunnah; the Hanafi school holds it obligatory for the one who recites or hears it. In a printed mushaf the places are marked, often with a line over the key word and a sign in the margin. There's a story in Bukhari: once the Prophet recited Surah an-Najm, and at its end he prostrated, and everyone with him prostrated too. And a hadith in Muslim says that when a person prostrates at such a verse, Satan withdraws, weeping, because he was commanded to bow and refused. The last sajdah in the book comes at the close of Surah al-'Alaq, the surah of the first revelation. In Pickthall's words: "Nay! Obey not thou him. But prostrate thyself, and draw near (unto Allah)." Prostrate, and draw near. That's the idea in one line: the lowest point of the body is the nearest point to God. There's even a surah named for it: Surah 32, as-Sajdah.
screen: `VERSES THAT SPEAK OF BOWING` · `FOURTEEN OR FIFTEEN PLACES` · `MARKED IN THE MARGIN` · `PROSTRATE, AND DRAW NEAR`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one prostration verse. After the bell, open a mushaf and look for the mark in the margin; the last verse of al-'Alaq is the easiest to find. For now, if you pray, you can make one prostration, forehead to the floor, and stay there for a few breaths. If you don't, simply lower your head, or rest your forehead on your hands, and notice how it feels to put the highest part of you at the lowest point. The bell holds the time.
Sajdah. A prostration, and the verses of the Qur'an where the reciter goes down to the ground. Today's word.

Your line: bow where it bows. Today, when something is bigger than you, a view, a kindness, a loss, let yourself be small in front of it for a moment instead of pushing back. Day three hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: When Muslims recite or hear one of the marked prostration verses, many make a single prostration on the spot, in prayer or outside it, and the whole congregation follows the imam when he does.
